slots.practicalActivity: Write a short answer to the lesson's check-yourself question: explain in your own words the difference between a physical bit sitting unread in memory and a classical probability distribution describing uncertainty about a bit, and state which one actually describes a real bit at rest.
slots.deliverable: A written paragraph distinguishing the physical-state view from the epistemic-probability view, with a clear final answer for the unread-bit case.

slots.practicalActivity: For |ψ⟩=(√3/2)|0⟩−(1/2)|1⟩, verify normalization by hand, compute P(0) and P(1), and write a short explanation of what role the minus sign plays even though it doesn't change either probability.
slots.deliverable: The normalization check, both computed probabilities, and a written explanation of the minus sign's role as a relative-phase fact.

lessons.title: Why Quantum Computers Are Not Just Faster Classical Computers

slots.practicalActivity: Write a rebuttal to a classmate who says 20 qubits in uniform superposition means 'simultaneously checking all 1,048,576 answers, so just measure it,' explaining specifically what's wrong with that plan and what would need to be added (interference engineering) before measuring could reliably reveal a useful answer.
slots.deliverable: A written rebuttal naming the measurement-collapse flaw in the plan and the interference-engineering step that's missing.

slots.practicalActivity: For a 4-qubit uniform superposition (16 equal amplitudes), compute by hand each amplitude's value, each outcome's probability, confirm the 16 probabilities sum to 1, and explain in writing why having 16 amplitudes doesn't mean a single measurement reveals more than 4 bits of information.
slots.deliverable: The computed amplitude (1/4) and probability (1/16) values, the sum-to-1 check, and a written explanation of the exponential-representation-vs-linear-readout gap.

lessons.title: The Pauli Gates: X, Y, Z

slots.practicalActivity: Start from (3/5)|0⟩+(4/5)|1⟩ and apply Z by hand, computing the resulting two amplitudes and the measurement probabilities for 0 and 1 both before and after Z, then explain in writing why an experimenter who can only measure (never compare state vectors) couldn't tell whether Z was applied.
slots.deliverable: The computed post-Z amplitudes, the matching before/after probabilities, and a written explanation of why the phase flip is invisible to measurement alone.

slots.practicalActivity: Starting from |1⟩, apply H, then Z, then H again. Using H²=I and what Z does to a |+⟩/|−⟩-style state (without computing the full matrix chain), reason through which single Pauli gate the sequence H·Z·H is equivalent to, then verify your answer with the actual matrix multiplication.
slots.deliverable: The reasoned prediction for H·Z·H and the matrix-multiplication verification confirming (or correcting) it.

slots.practicalActivity: If you apply T six times in a row to |1⟩, compute the resulting phase angle in degrees (using T's 45° step), and determine which gate from this chapter (X, Y, Z, H, S, T) produces that exact same phase angle in a single application, explaining your reasoning using the eighth-turn relationships.
slots.deliverable: The computed phase angle after six T applications and a written identification of the matching single gate, with reasoning shown.

slots.practicalActivity: Compute Ry(π)|0⟩ by hand using the Ry matrix, then compare it entry by entry to X|0⟩, and determine whether Ry(π) equals X outright, equals X only up to a global phase, or is genuinely different, following the same comparison method the lesson used for Rx(π) vs. X.
slots.deliverable: The computed Ry(π)|0⟩ vector, the entry-by-entry comparison to X|0⟩, and a written verdict (equal, equal up to global phase, or different).

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lab's own three-step method, compute what happens when you apply S, then H, then S again, to |0⟩: write the intermediate state after each gate, then the final amplitudes and probabilities, and compare the final result to the H-S-H example's answer to determine whether the two sequences are equivalent.
slots.deliverable: The full step-by-step state trace for S-H-S on |0⟩ and a written comparison concluding whether it matches the lesson's H-S-H result.

slots.practicalActivity: Starting from |11⟩, apply CNOT(control=q1,target=q2), then apply a second CNOT(control=q2,target=q1) to the result, using the basis-state flip rule (not full matrix multiplication). State the final 2-qubit state and whether it matches leaving |11⟩ untouched.
slots.deliverable: The two-step basis-state trace and a written conclusion on whether the combined operation reproduces the identity on |11⟩.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the block-form controlled-U recipe, write out the full 4x4 matrix for controlled-Y (control=q1, target=q2) using the Pauli-Y matrix, then predict term by term what this gate does to the basis state |10⟩.
slots.deliverable: The full 4x4 controlled-Y matrix and the predicted (and verified) output of applying it to |10⟩.

slots.practicalActivity: Evaluate a classmate's claim that 'SWAP applied twice always returns the original state, so SWAP is its own inverse,' using either the explicit SWAP matrix or the three-CNOT decomposition to justify your answer in writing.
slots.deliverable: A written justification (using the matrix or the CNOT decomposition) confirming or correcting the claim that SWAP is self-inverse.

slots.practicalActivity: Starting from |11⟩, apply H to qubit 1, then CNOT with control=q1, target=q2, and using the H+CNOT recipe table from the lesson (not a fresh matrix computation), predict which of the four Bell states you land on and its four measurement probabilities, then verify by computing the actual amplitudes.
slots.deliverable: The predicted Bell state from the recipe table and the verified amplitude computation confirming (or correcting) the prediction, with the four measurement probabilities.

slots.practicalActivity: Starting from |00⟩, apply CNOT with control=q1, target=q2 first, and only then apply H to qubit 1 (the reverse order from the standard Bell-state recipe). Compute the resulting state step by step and determine whether it's the same Bell state, a different one, or not entangled at all.
slots.deliverable: The step-by-step state computation for the reversed gate order and a written verdict on which state, if any Bell state, results.

slots.practicalActivity: Draw the circuit diagram, in the same ASCII style as the lesson, for a 2-qubit circuit that starts from |00⟩, applies X to qubit 2, then H to qubit 1, then CNOT with qubit 1 as control and qubit 2 as target. Reading your own diagram left to right, state which gate happens first in time and on which qubit.
slots.deliverable: The drawn ASCII circuit diagram and a written statement identifying the first gate in time order.

slots.practicalActivity: For a 4-qubit circuit with H on q1, H on q3 (same layer), then CNOT(control=q1,target=q2) and separately CNOT(control=q3,target=q4), with the two CNOTs sharing no qubit with each other, determine the circuit's width and depth and state which gates share a layer with which.
slots.deliverable: The computed width and depth values and a written layer-by-layer breakdown of which gates run together.

slots.practicalActivity: Given that S=T·T exactly and S²=Z, determine how many T gates applied in sequence exactly reproduce the Z gate, reasoning from those two given facts alone without computing a fresh matrix product.
slots.deliverable: A written derivation, using S=T² and S²=Z, concluding the exact number of T applications that reproduce Z.

lessons.title: Designing a Circuit From a Specification

slots.practicalActivity: Using the same workflow as the lesson (known recipe, identify the gap, propose a gate, verify numerically), determine what single gate change to the verified H-Z-CNOT sequence would instead produce (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 again, reasoning from what Z does and checking your answer against the Chapter 3 original result.
slots.deliverable: A written proposal for the gate change and a verification argument confirming it restores the original Bell state.

slots.practicalActivity: For the lab's Problem 1 verified circuit (X on q2, H on q1, then CNOT), compute the circuit's width and depth using the same layer-counting method as the earlier depth-and-width lesson, showing which gates occupy which layer.
slots.deliverable: The computed width and depth for the Problem 1 circuit with a written layer breakdown.

lessons.title: Building the Teleportation Circuit
lessons.chapterTitle: Quantum Teleportation & Superdense Coding in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: Suppose Alice measures q1=1, q2=1 (outcome '11') but the classical message to Bob is lost. Using the raw uncorrected amplitudes Bob holds, (-0.3, 0.4), explain concretely what Bob can and can't determine about |ψ⟩ from his qubit alone, and why no randomly guessed correction fixes it reliably.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of what information is and isn't recoverable from Bob's uncorrected qubit, and why random guessing fails.

lessons.title: Building the Superdense Coding Circuit
lessons.chapterTitle: Quantum Teleportation & Superdense Coding in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: Work through what happens if Alice encodes '10' with Z but Bob's qubit q2 was accidentally measured (destroying the entanglement) before Alice's qubit arrives. Explain in writing, using the fact that a measured/disentangled q2 can no longer meaningfully receive Bob's CNOT, why the decode procedure can no longer reliably recover Alice's 2 bits.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of why premature measurement of q2 breaks the decode step and destroys recoverability of the message.

lessons.title: Why These Protocols Don't Violate No-Cloning
lessons.chapterTitle: Quantum Teleportation & Superdense Coding in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: Write a precise rebuttal to a skeptic who argues 'Alice's measurement instantly determines Bob's state, so information traveled faster than light,' using the fact that Bob's qubit is indistinguishable from a maximally mixed state until the classical bits arrive.
slots.deliverable: A written rebuttal explaining precisely where the skeptic's faster-than-light argument fails, citing the maximally-mixed-until-classical-bits-arrive fact.

lessons.title: Teleportation & Coding Lab
lessons.chapterTitle: Quantum Teleportation & Superdense Coding in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: Using the same method as the lesson's Problem 1, trace the |+⟩=(1/√2)|0⟩+(1/√2)|1⟩ state through the full teleportation circuit, noting that two of the four correction branches will look identical in their raw amplitudes before correction. Work out all four branches and confirm each corrects to exactly |+⟩.
slots.deliverable: The full four-branch teleportation trace for |+⟩, including the raw and corrected amplitudes for each branch, confirming all four converge to |+⟩.

slots.practicalActivity: For a 4-qubit system (16 amplitudes, qubits numbered 1-4 left to right), determine which bit position the mask needs to target to apply X to qubit 3, and work out at least two concrete pairs of the 16 indices that would get swapped.
slots.deliverable: The identified bit position/mask for qubit 3 and at least two worked index pairs showing the swap.

lessons.title: Why Simulators Don't Scale: the Exponential Wall

slots.practicalActivity: Using the 2^n × 16-byte formula, extend the lesson's table by doubling twice from the n=50 row to compute the memory requirement for a 52-qubit state vector, and name which storage unit (GB/TB/PB/EB) that number lands in.
slots.deliverable: The computed byte count for n=52 and the correctly identified storage-unit tier.

lessons.title: Simulator vs. Real Hardware: What Changes

slots.practicalActivity: Reasoning from the lesson's 1,000-shot Bell-state simulation (487/513 instead of exactly 500/500), predict whether running the same circuit for only 10 shots would land closer to or farther from a clean 50/50 split, and explain why using what you know about finite-sampling noise.
slots.deliverable: A written prediction (farther from 50/50) with a statistical explanation grounded in smaller sample size producing larger relative sampling noise.

lessons.title: Capstone: Build a Circuit Simulator Core

slots.practicalActivity: Using the applySingleQubitGate function exactly as written in this lesson's simulator core, determine whether you could add an S gate without changing the function itself, then identify specifically what would stop you from adding a true complex-valued Y gate and what part of the state representation would need to change to support it.
slots.deliverable: A written answer confirming S can be added as-is since its real diagonal entries fit the existing real-array representation, and identifying the real-to-complex-number representation change needed to support Y.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can read and design real quantum circuits from scratch — applying the Pauli, Hadamard, phase, rotation, CNOT, SWAP, and Toffoli gates by hand; building and verifying Bell states, teleportation, and superdense coding circuits with real computed amplitudes; and has built their own working state-vector circuit simulator core, the same architecture production tools like Qiskit's Aer use internally.
